The Bad Creek Project dams would be founded on residual soils which have an adequate shear strength to support the imposed loads. A large number of tests will be required to determine the permeability of the soil and rock foundations. The natural materials available for construction appear marginal and would require careful design and proper construction control.
Seepage losses through the foundation rock are another item of concern. Grouting is planned in the creek bottom, and soil blanketing is planned where the soil cover over weathered rock is relatively thin. Along portions of the proposed reservoir rim, the thickness of the confining ridges is less than desirable. Foundation treatment would be required to reduce seepage losses and insure stability. If reservoir seepage contributes to the flows along adjacent drainages, it may prove essential to control these discharges and potential sedimentation problems, which could result from such flows.
For the most part, anticipated drawdown slides would not create engineering problems. After a few seasons of operation, the steeper reservoir rim slopes would degrade to more stable, flatter slopes. The amount of displaced reservoir storage would be negligible. Maintenance and access roads should be located far enough landward from the reservoir to anticipate these slides. At a few narrow rim locations, more positive slope stabilization measures would be required to avoid drawdown slides which could endanger the reservoir. Associated with the slides during the first few seasons of operation would be turbid water.
Information on the mineral resources in the project area is based on a literature search, field reconnaissance, and results of foundation investigations for the Bad Creek structures and reservoir rim. According to Cazeau (1967), Oconee County can be divided into five major rock zones, designated on the basis of dominant or typical lithology. The zones strike northeast and dip to the southeast. From northwest to southeast the zones are (1) mica gneiss zone, (2) Brevard schist zone, (3) augen gneiss zone, (4) hornblende gneiss injection zone, and (5) biotite gneiss zone. The Bad Creek Project is located in the mica gneiss zone, which is defined to include all rocks lying northwest of the Brevard belt in Oconee County. Granite is the principal natural resource of Oconee County and occurs in every lithologic zone except the Brevard belt; however, there are no active quarries in the project area.
